la:verb:coquo.html:
cŏquo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a.
kindr. with Sanscr. pak; Gr. πεπ in πέπτω or πέσσω; Germ. backen; Engl. bake
,
to cook, to prepare by cooking, to bake, boil, roast, parch, steep, melt, heat (very freq. and class.).
Lit.: cenam,; : cottidie sic cena ei coquebatur, ut, etc.,: cibum,; cf. cibaria,; ; ; 44, 35, 13 al.: qui illa coxerat,: quae coxerat aere cavo,: dulce dedit, tostā quod coxerat ante polentā,cooked from parched malt,: humana exta,: (pavonem),: aliquid ex oleo,in oil,; so, aliquid ex aceto,. —Absol.: si nusquam coctum is, quidnam cenat Juppiter?: in nonum diem solet ire coctum,; : coquendo sit faxo et molendo,.—
Subst.
coctum, i, n., cooked food: quid tu, malum, curas, utrum crudum an coctum edim? Ussing: ne quid in popinas cocti praeter legumina aut olera veniret,.— Plur.: cocta vendere,.—
cocta, ae, f., water boiled, and cooled by ice; a decoction, ; cf. ; .—
Transf.
To prepare by fire, to burn, parch, etc.: laterculos,: calcem, sq.: carbonem,fin.: locum sol,; cf.: glaebas maturis solibus aestas,: cocta ligna,dried, hardened by drying,: coctus agger,i. e. built of bricks,rosaria cocta matutino Noto,dried up, parched,; cf.: at vos, praesentes Austri, coquite horum obsonia,: aurum cum plumbo,: aera fornacibus,.—
To ripen, make mature: arbores sol ac luna,: uvas,; cf. vinum,; and: mitis vindemia,: poma (with matura),: fructus solibus,: messem,—
= concoquo, to digest: cibus confectus jam coctusque,; (but in these passages Madv. ad , would read concoquo, denying that coquo ever means to digest; cf. Spald. ad ); Lact. Opif. Dei, 14, 5; cf.: balineae ardentes, quibus persuasere in corporibus cibos coqui,: plerique ... bubulum coquunt,; .—
Trop. (in the poets and prose writers after the Aug. per.).
To elaborate something in mind, to consider, to think, meditate upon, contrive, plan: quicquid est, incoctum non expromet; bene coctum dabit,: bene cocto, condito, sermone bono, Lucil. ap. ; cf. ; cf.: consilia secreto,: bellum,: trucem invidiam,: iras cum fraude,: Latio extrema coepta,.—
To vex, harass, torment, disturb the mind: egomet me coquo et macero et defetigo,: si quid ego adjuero curamve levasso, quae nunc te coquit et versat in pectore fixa, Enn. ap. ; cf.: si sollicitudo oratorem macerat et coquit,: quos ira metusque coquebat,: quam ... Femineae ardentem curaeque iraeque coquebant,.—Hence, Ital. cuocere; Fr. cuire.—Hence, coctus, a, um, P. a. (acc. to III. A. supra), well considered, well digested: bene coctus sermo, Lucil. ap. .—Transf., of persons: hodie juris coctiores non sunt, qui lites creant. Quam, etc. (alluding to the double meaning of jus), better skilled in, etc., .

la:noun:coquus.gloss: A cook; person who makes food.
senses: A cook; person who makes food.
la:noun:coquus.html:
cŏquus (ante-class. cŏquŏs; in many MSS. and inscrr. also cŏcus), i, m.,
a cook (very freq., esp. in Plaut., in whose comedies the cook takes a conspicuous place), ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.—In ancient times the cook baked also the bread; cf. Naev. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 58, 14 Müll.—From the ancient writing, quoquus for cocus, originates the pun upon the voc. coque and quoque, Cic. ap. Spald.

senses: of or pertaining to the kitchen

,

A kitchen, ; ; .—
